question: What is the Definition of Done, and what happens to a Product Backlog item that doesn't meet it?
text:
The Definition of Done (DoD) is a formal description of the state of the product Increment when it satisfies the required quality measures for the product[1]. It creates transparency by establishing a shared, agreed-upon understanding among the Scrum Team and stakeholders regarding what functional and non-functional work was completed for a work item[1][2]. The exact moment a Product Backlog item meets the Definition of Done, a usable product Increment is born[1][3].
If organizational quality standards exist, the team must adopt them as a minimum baseline; otherwise, the Scrum Team creates a Definition of Done tailored to the product, which Developers are required to conform to[1][4].
What Happens to an Item That Doesn't Meet the Definition of Done?
When a Product Backlog item does not meet the Definition of Done by the end of a Sprint:
It cannot be released or presented: The item cannot be released to production, nor can it be presented/demonstrated at the Sprint Review[1][5]. This maintains transparency and prevents creating a false impression of progress[5].
It returns to the Product Backlog: The item is placed back into the Product Backlog for future re-prioritization, refinement, and consideration in upcoming Sprint Planning sessions[1].
No partial credit is awarded: No partial story points or fractional progress are credited to the completed Sprint for unfinished work[6]. The Product Owner and team re-evaluate the item's remaining scope and priority empirically[6].
💡 Would you like to explore how the Definition of Done differs from Acceptance Criteria, or discuss techniques for facilitating a team session to create one?

Increment
An Increment is a concrete stepping stone toward the Product Goal. Each Increment is additive to all
prior Increments and thoroughly verified, ensuring that all Increments work together. In order to
provide value, the Increment must be usable.

Tips  
• This is not a status meeting. Rather, it is an opportunity for stakeholders to collaborate with the team and improve the Product Backlog with shared context and learnings.
• Don’t demonstrate work that isn’t “ Done .” It can significantly erode trust between the Scrum Team , stakeholders, and end users if the demonstrated work doesn’t get shipped as expected. It also allows the Scrum Team to persist the illusion that incomplete work is still valuable. Remember: work in process is a liability, not an asset. ( ap.tips/toc )

• 5 minutes: Check in with everyone socially, especially if you are a distributed team.
• 5 minutes: If your team hasn’t done so already, review incomplete Backlog Items from the
